prohibited_recommendations: Do not give IV thrombolysis in suspected infective endocarditis: it increases intracranial haemorrhage (AHA/ASA 2026, COR 3: Harm).
Do not start anticoagulant or antiplatelet therapy for the stroke in infective endocarditis: it does not prevent embolism and adds haemorrhage risk, including from an infectious aneurysm.
Do not start antibiotics before the blood culture sets are drawn, unless the patient is haemodynamically unstable.

Do not start or restart antihypertensive treatment in the first 48 to 72 hours for blood pressure below 220/120 mmHg in a patient who receives neither IV thrombolysis nor thrombectomy and has no comorbid indication; it does not prevent death or dependency (AHA/ASA 2026, COR 3: No Benefit).
Do not delay non-contrast CT for additional imaging or labs in a stroke alert presentation.
required_recommendations: Establish last known well (sudden onset at home, about 3 hours before arrival) and the NIHSS (7).
Obtain non-contrast CT head first to exclude intracranial haemorrhage before any thrombolytic decision.
Verify glucose to exclude hypoglycaemia as a stroke mimic.

IV thrombolysis: do not give, because the presentation is suspected infective endocarditis (fever, Osler nodes, Janeway lesions, Roth spots, splinter haemorrhages, aortic regurgitation murmur on a bicuspid valve), in which it increases intracranial haemorrhage (AHA/ASA 2026, COR 3: Harm), although onset is within 4.5 hours. Thrombectomy: not indicated, because CTA shows no large vessel occlusion.
Draw three sets of blood cultures from separate venepunctures before the first antibiotic dose.

Start IV antibiotics once the cultures are drawn; for the penicillin-susceptible oral streptococcus (Streptococcus mutans, penicillin MIC 0.06 mg/L) on a native valve, give IV benzylpenicillin or ceftriaxone for 4 weeks (ESC 2023).

Diagnose definite infective endocarditis by the Duke criteria: two major (typical organism in all blood culture sets, vegetation on echocardiography) with minor criteria (predisposing bicuspid valve, fever, embolic and immunological phenomena).
Obtain a transoesophageal echocardiogram although the transthoracic study shows the vegetation, to define vegetation size and mobility and detect perivalvular complications (ESC 2023).
Screen for infectious (mycotic) intracranial aneurysm with CTA or MRA, and repeat vascular imaging if headache, new deficit or haemorrhage occurs.

Refer urgently to the endocarditis team with cardiac surgery: a mobile 1.8 cm aortic vegetation that has embolised, with moderate aortic regurgitation, raises the indication for early surgery, and an ischaemic stroke without haemorrhage or coma does not by itself justify delaying it (ESC 2023).
Admit to a stroke unit with continuous cardiac monitoring (telemetry); a new AV block or PR prolongation signals a perivalvular abscess and calls for repeat ECG and echocardiography.
Do not start antiplatelet or anticoagulant therapy for the stroke; embolic risk is reduced by antibiotics and, where indicated, surgery.
Stop ibuprofen; use paracetamol for fever and pain.
Arrange dental assessment to treat the oral source of infection.
Explain that after this episode he is in the highest-risk group (previous endocarditis) and needs a single antibiotic dose before future dental procedures.

Six weeks of fever, night sweats and 8 kg weight loss after a dental extraction, with Osler nodes, Janeway lesions, Roth spots, splinter haemorrhages, an aortic regurgitation murmur and a wide pulse pressure on a known bicuspid aortic valve: subacute infective endocarditis.

Definite endocarditis by the Duke criteria: Streptococcus mutans in all three blood culture sets and a 1.8 cm aortic vegetation (two major), with a predisposing valve, fever 38.4, embolic events and immunological phenomena (Osler nodes, Roth spots, glomerulonephritis with RBC casts).
Thrombolysis is harmful in suspected infective endocarditis (COR 3: Harm) even within 4.5 hours, and CTA shows no occlusion for thrombectomy; no antithrombotic is started for the stroke.

TEE is recommended even after a positive TTE to detect perivalvular complications (ESC 2023); here it shows a mobile 1.8 x 0.7 cm vegetation without abscess, and telemetry shows no new conduction block.
A large mobile aortic vegetation that has already embolised raises the indication for early surgery; an ischaemic stroke without haemorrhage or coma does not by itself delay it.

Antibiotic prophylaxis before dental procedures is not recommended for a bicuspid aortic valve without previous endocarditis (AHA 2021 statement), so the untaken amoxicillin dose was not indicated; the extraction is the likely portal of entry, and after this episode he is in the highest-risk group.

AHA/ASA 2026 sequencing: glucose is checked before thrombolysis, but routine CBC/coagulation results are not awaited without a reason to expect abnormality; ECG/troponin do not delay reperfusion, and CTA/CTP do not wait for creatinine.

clinical_pearls: Multiple acute infarcts in several arterial territories of both hemispheres on DWI suggest a central embolic source; with fever, endocarditis comes first.
IV thrombolysis is harmful in endocarditis-related stroke because septic arteritis and infectious aneurysms raise the risk of intracranial haemorrhage.
Bicuspid aortic valve is the most common congenital cardiac anomaly (1-2% of the population) and predisposes to infective endocarditis, but it is not an indication for dental antibiotic prophylaxis.
In the Duke criteria, a typical organism in multiple blood cultures plus echocardiographic evidence of a vegetation are two major criteria and establish definite endocarditis.
TEE is recommended in suspected endocarditis even after a positive TTE, to detect perivalvular abscess, pseudoaneurysm and perforation.
Infectious intracranial aneurysms are uncommon, usually on distal MCA branches, and may appear after the first vascular study.
metadata.difficulty_description: Diagnostic puzzle: 41-year-old musician with 6 weeks of fever, weight loss and night sweats after a dental extraction, now presenting with an acute right MCA stroke. Multi-territory infarcts on MRI reveal an embolic shower from Streptococcus mutans endocarditis on a bicuspid aortic valve. Requires recognizing the systemic and peripheral signs of endocarditis, withholding thrombolysis, drawing blood cultures before antibiotics, proceeding from TTE to TEE, and screening for infectious aneurysm.
metadata.difficulty_rationale: Septic embolism from infective endocarditis on a bicuspid aortic valve: fever, dental portal of entry, multi-territory embolic pattern; thrombolysis is harmful; early surgery and infectious aneurysm are the management questions.

patient.history_present_illness: Mr. Marcus Everett is a 41-year-old right-handed African American man who is a freelance jazz saxophonist, presenting to the emergency department via EMS with acute-onset left-sided weakness beginning approximately 3 hours ago. He was at home preparing for an evening performance when he suddenly noticed his left arm felt heavy and clumsy. Within minutes, his left leg became weak and he was unable to stand without support. A friend who was visiting called 911. On further history, the patient reports that for the past 6 weeks he has been experiencing intermittent low-grade fevers, drenching night sweats, progressive fatigue, poor appetite, and an unintentional 8 kg weight loss. He attributed these symptoms to his demanding performance schedule and a persistent 'flu' that he could not shake. He notes generalized joint aches, particularly in his knees and wrists, that began approximately 4 weeks ago. Two weeks ago he noticed painful red bumps on the pads of his left index and middle fingers, which he thought were from playing saxophone. He also noticed small dark streaks under his fingernails. He has not sought medical attention for these symptoms. He had a dental extraction 8 weeks ago; his dentist had prescribed a single dose of amoxicillin to take before the procedure, which he did not take. He has a known bicuspid aortic valve discovered 5 years ago, which he was told was benign and required no treatment or follow-up. He explicitly denies any intravenous drug use, past or present. He denies chest pain, frank dyspnea, or lower extremity edema, though he has noticed becoming winded more easily during saxophone performances in the past few weeks. He has had no prior strokes, seizures, or neurological symptoms.
